summary:
Flame in Freefall: Space Fire Safety Simulation
Flame in Freefall investigates how fires behave aboard spacecraft under microgravity conditions and aims to improve crew safety. Based on NASA research, it provides an SI-powered simulator to assess fire risks and evaluate emergency responses.

Users can adjust oxygen concentration, pressure, gravity and ventilation, then select from 23 materials and ignite a sample. The system monitors flame behaviour, heat release rate, gas emissions and an SI risk score.

In microgravity, reduced natural convection means oxygen reaches flames mainly by diffusion. This can produce spherical flames, while changes in airflow can alter their shape and development.

The simulator analyses carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and other combustion gases to assess toxic gas accumulation in enclosed spaces. A flame disappearing does not necessarily mean the danger has passed: harmful gases and combustion may persist.

Using comparisons with NASA experiments, including Saffire, the project evaluates measures such as stopping ventilation, applying carbon dioxide and evacuating the spacecraft. Its aim is to support fire prevention, early detection, effective suppression and protection of crew members from smoke and toxic gases.
details:
Flame in Freefall is an interactive web simulation that models solid fuel combustion, pyrolysis gas emissions (such as CO, CO₂, HCN), and thermal behavior under microgravity ($\mu g$) versus Earth ($1g$) conditions. Inspired by NASA's Saffire and FLEX microgravity experiments, our project addresses critical fire safety challenges in confined spacecraft environments where traditional $1g$ intuitions fail. The platform features vertical channel thermal propagation profiles based on material ignition temperature ($T_{ig}$), real-time toxic gas concentration (ppm) and yield ($g/kg$) tracking, and comparative live SI risk analysis ($0-100$) paired with emergency intervention recommendations. Equipped with a secure, offline-capable AI assistant powered by local Ollama (Qwen 2.5) architecture, the project was developed using HTML5 Canvas, JavaScript, NASA WSTF flammability data, the SFPE Handbook (Tewarson tables), and ICES exploration atmosphere reports.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI) *

Super Intelligence (SI) tools were actively utilized in the project for code writing, data analysis, and powering the assistant component. Local large language models (Ollama / Qwen 2.5) were integrated to provide real-time conversational analysis and safety recommendations regarding spacecraft fire dynamics and gas emissions, while AI also assisted in optimizing the HTML5 Canvas simulation engine and physical models. All interface components and code architecture were structured in accordance with NASA Space Apps Challenge transparency guidelines.
